questions.prompt: On this T2-weighted prostate MRI, click the peripheral zone.
questions.hint: The crescent at the back and sides of the gland, bright on T2.
questions.explain: The peripheral zone is the bright, glandular crescent posterior and lateral to the transition zone on T2 images, and it is where about 70 percent of prostate cancers arise. A focal dark area within it is the typical appearance of a tumour on PI-RADS reading.

questions.prompt: On this T2-weighted prostate MRI, click the transition zone.
questions.hint: The central part of the gland around the urethra, darker and more heterogeneous than the rim around it.
questions.explain: The transition zone surrounds the proximal urethra and enlarges with benign prostatic hyperplasia, giving a heterogeneous nodular appearance on T2. Tumours here are harder to see, so diffusion imaging adds the most value in this zone.

questions.prompt: A 66-year-old has a PSA of 9 ng/mL. On MRI there is a focal, lens-shaped dark area in the part of the gland that is normally bright on T2, with restricted diffusion. Click the zone where this lesion sits.
questions.hint: The bright crescent at the back of the gland.
questions.explain: A focal hypointense lesion in the normally bright peripheral zone with restricted diffusion is the classic PI-RADS 4 to 5 appearance of a clinically significant cancer, and the target for MRI-guided biopsy.

questions.prompt: A 72-year-old has nocturia, a weak stream and a smoothly enlarged gland on examination. MRI shows a markedly enlarged central gland with well-defined nodules and a thinned bright rim. Click the zone that has enlarged.
questions.hint: The central part of the gland around the urethra.
questions.explain: Benign prostatic hyperplasia enlarges the transition zone, which compresses the peripheral zone into a thin bright rim on T2. Encapsulated nodules with a mix of bright and dark signal are typical of BPH rather than cancer.
